name: Platelet PGD2 inhibitors

lead: PGD2 inhibitors target a signalling molecule found at about three times higher levels in bald scalp than haired scalp. Blocking its receptor, GPR44 (DP2), is proposed to let follicles regrow.
The lead drug, setipiprant, reached a phase 2A hair-loss trial; no statistically significant improvement was reported in 2018.

paras: PGD2 acts through GPR44/DP2 to slow hair growth in cultured human follicles and mice. A DP2 antagonist blocks that receptor, working apart from the DHT pathway targeted by finasteride.
No hair-loss product is approved. Setipiprant showed no severe adverse effects in phase II and III data and no difference from placebo. Gray-market or homemade versions are unregulated.

Miniaturised follicles could regrow thicker hair
angle.text: People interested in hair regrowth follow PGD2 inhibition as a route that works separately from DHT blockers such as finasteride. The goal is thicker, denser hair on balding scalp.

lead: Prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) inhibitors are an experimental hair-loss approach that aims to block a signal that holds hair follicles back, with the goal of reversing miniaturisation and restoring thicker hair on balding scalp. The idea comes from a 2012 study led by Luis Garza and George Cotsarelis at the University of Pennsylvania, which found PGD2 in bald scalp of men with androgenetic alopecia at about three times the level of haired scalp.[1]

In that work PGD2 and its derivative 15-dPGJ2 slowed hair growth in cultured human follicles and in mice, acting through the receptor GPR44 (also called DP2 or CRTH2).[1][2] The authors proposed that blocking this receptor could be a treatment target in men and women.[1]

The pathway is separate from the DHT mechanism targeted by finasteride and dutasteride, which is why it attracts interest from people whose hair loss continues despite those drugs. Prostaglandin D2 is also known outside hair as a major mast-cell product involved in asthma and allergy, which is why DP2-blocking drugs were already in development when the hair link was reported.[2]

The oral DP2 antagonist setipiprant was taken into a phase 2A hair-loss trial after the finding; it did not show a statistically significant improvement.[3] Topical and other DP2-targeting compounds, and platelet-derived preparations that people link to prostaglandin pathways, remain a community topic rather than an established treatment.

paras: PGD2 is a lipid signalling molecule made by the enzyme PGD2 synthase. Another prostaglandin, F2-alpha, is known to promote hair growth, and Penn researchers described prostaglandins as acting in opposition on hair.[1] Elevated PGD2 and its synthase in bald scalp follicles may partly explain male-pattern hair loss.[2]

PGD2 is a major prostaglandin produced by mast cells and binds to the receptors DP1 (PTGDR) and DP2 (CRTH2, also called GPR44). It is produced through the arachidonic acid cascade, with PGD2 synthase converting PGH2 to PGD2.[2] Wikipedia describes the 2012 paper as indicating a causal link between elevated local PGD2 and hair growth inhibition: topical PGD2 prevented hair growth, mice genetically inclined to produce more PGD2 showed inhibited hair growth, and bald scalp tissue had much higher PGD2 and PGD2 synthase than non-bald tissue.[2] The paper proposed that PGD2 acts at the DP2 receptor, making it a therapeutic target in men and women.[2]

PGD2 is also known as the primary mediator of the niacin flush, according to research from 1989 summarised on Wikipedia, and its levels in asthma patients are reported to be about ten times higher than in controls.[2]

A phase 2A trial of oral setipiprant against placebo (NCT02781311) in men aged 18 to 49 with androgenetic alopecia completed in May 2018 without a statistically significant improvement.[3] Setipiprant itself was developed first for asthma by Actelion; rights for hair loss passed to Kythera and then Allergan.[3] Another DP2 antagonist, fevipiprant, was developed for asthma by Novartis and discontinued in 2019 after phase III trials, and was not studied for hair loss.[4] Setipiprant was first developed for asthma, where trials found it well tolerated and reasonably effective at reducing allergen-induced airway responses, and development there was discontinued because it offered no clear advantage over existing drugs.[3] Reported pharmacokinetics include a human half-life of about 11 hours and peak plasma levels 1.8 to 4 hours after an oral dose.[3]
In phase II and III data setipiprant showed no severe adverse effects and no pattern different from placebo.[3]

Beyond oral DP2 antagonists, the in silico literature on Wikipedia lists predicted inhibitors of PGD2 synthase including acteoside, amentoflavone, rutin and hinokiflavone, and describes vitamin K and vitamin D3 as natural inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis; these have not been tested for hair growth.[2] The 2012 authors suggested prostaglandin signalling may be a shared pathway in male and female androgenetic alopecia.[1]

The 2012 study was led by Luis Garza, then a Penn postdoctoral fellow, with senior author George Cotsarelis, chair of dermatology at the Perelman School of Medicine. The team compared scalp tissue from balding and non-balding areas of men with male pattern baldness without a preset hypothesis, then checked the finding in mice and in cultured follicles.[1] PGD2 was about three times higher in bald scalp, PGD2 shortened growth in cultured follicles, and its derivative 15-dPGJ2 completely blocked growth through GPR44.[1] Cotsarelis said prostaglandins had not been thought about in relation to hair loss.[1] The authors suggested topical GPR44-targeting treatments and testing in women as next steps.[1]

The pathway was reported in Science Translational Medicine in March 2012; Garza and Cotsarelis are co-inventors on a Penn patent describing PGD2 as a target for inhibiting hair loss.[1] Kythera acquired setipiprant for baldness after the paper, and Allergan took over development in 2015.[3]

timeline.event: Penn researchers report elevated PGD2 in bald scalp and inhibition via GPR44.[1]
Allergan acquires Kythera and continues setipiprant for hair loss.[3]
Phase 2A setipiprant trial completes without a statistically significant result.[3]
